newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos says disappointed on Manila Hotel verdict.
newsitem.headline: Ramos says disappointed on Manila Hotel verdict.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Tuesday the Philippines' privatisation programme suffered a blow when the Supreme Court cancelled the winning bid of a Malaysian firm for the renowned Manila Hotel.
"To tell you frankly, I'm very disappointed. We have lost so much time and (it is)...going to set back our privatisation programme," Ramos told a news conference in this central Philippine town.
"This will impact in a negative way upon our pro-poor programme and our policy to attract more outside investors, including our own domestic investors, into our privatisation programme," he added.

The Supreme Court on Monday threw out the winning bid of Renong Berhad and ordered the Government Service and Insurance System, the owner of the Manila Hotel, to sell the property to local firm Manila Prince Hotel Corporation in accordance with a "Filipino First" policy.

Manila Prince lost the bidding to Renong in 1995 but subsequently offered to match the winning bid and petitioned the Supreme Court for the contract, saying the Manila Hotel was a national treasure that should not be handed over to a foreign entity.
Ramos hinted the government might appeal against the decision.
"The best government can do is to submit a petition for reconsideration," he said without confirming that it would in fact do so.

"We are not questioning the opinion of the Supreme Court. We honour it...but it must be understood that the Ramos government is responsible enough and we have shown it by our record to protect our history... and we do not just casually or whimsically or irresponsibly dispose of our national patrimony just like that," Ramos added.
Last week, the Court of Appeals temporarily halted the privatisation of Manila's Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) after the winning bidders were announced.
The court was responding to a petition by a citizens' group which said Ramos's authority to privatise the utility had lapsed.
Analysts have said an increasing tendency of resorting to courts after high-profile projects have been awarded could scare away foreign investors.
They have said it could have a significant effect on the Philippines' efforts to upgrade its creaking infrastructure through privatisations.
